Common age effect model for several populations

Source: R/model-cae.R
cae.Rd

Joint model of the strata as populations that share their age effects and keep their own period effects: the common age effect (CAE) model of Kleinow (2015). Status: published. The model and its estimation follow Kleinow (2015), and section and equation numbers refer to that paper unless another is named; index = "coherent" forecasts with the model of Enchev, Kleinow and Cairns (2017); the default forecast and the other choices listed below are package-specific.

Usage

cae(order = 1, common_by = NULL, index = c("rwd", "coherent"))

Arguments

order

Number of common age effects (p in the paper).

common_by

Stratum variable(s) defining groups of strata with their own common age effects (package-specific, see Details).

index

Time-series model of the period effects: "rwd" (one multivariate random walk with a drift for every population and order, package-specific) or "coherent" (a common drift for the first period effects and mean-reverting autoregressions for the others; Enchev, Kleinow and Cairns 2017). See Details.

Value

A model specification. The fit (fit$fits) holds the common age effects beta (one matrix per group), the centring a [age, stratum], the period effects kappa [order, year, stratum], the drift drift, the autoregressive coefficient phi (1 for a random walk) and the innovation covariance sigma of the stacked period effects (order within stratum), the common drift of each group common_drift (index = "coherent"), mse and bic.

Details

Model (Sections 2 and 3.1, eq. 1-3). The log death rates y[x, t, i] = log(D[x, t, i] / E[x, t, i]) of each population i are centred over the years: m[x, t, i] = y[x, t, i] - a[x, i], with a[x, i] the mean over the years. The centred rates follow m[, , i] = beta kappa[, , i] + e[, , i]. The age effects beta (ages x order) are common to all populations; the period effects kappa[, , i] (order x years) belong to each population. With one population the model is the Lee-Carter model with order age-period terms, estimated by a singular value decomposition; for order = 1 it gives the fitted rates and forecasts of lee_carter(method = "svd", adjust = "none").

Identification (Section 2). The columns of beta have length 1 and are orthogonal to each other. The period effects of each population sum to zero over the years, because the rates are centred. The sign of each column of beta is chosen so that its sum is positive (package-specific).

Estimation (Section 3.2). With Q[i] = m[, , i] t(m[, , i]), beta is the orthogonal matrix that minimises the sum over populations of the squared off-diagonal elements of t(beta) Q[i] beta: the paper's least-squares modification of the common principal component analysis of Flury (1984). Every population has the same weight whatever its size, as in the paper, which prefers this to maximum likelihood because large populations would dominate the age effects. The first order columns are kept, and kappa[, , i] = t(beta) m[, , i]. The paper requires more years than age groups (Section 2), and so does cae(): with fewer years, use wider age groups (mt_regroup()) or fewer ages (mt_subset()); Kleinow fitted ages 18-52 and 53-87 separately.

Forecasts. Kleinow (2015) does not forecast. index chooses the time-series model of the period effects. Both models start from the fitted rates of the last year, as in Enchev, Kleinow and Cairns (2017, Section 6.3) (anchored() starts them from the observed rates), and keep a and beta fixed. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates and the exposures (Kleinow makes no assumption about the distribution of the errors).

  • index = "rwd" (default, package-specific): the period effects of all populations and orders follow one multivariate random walk with drift, kappa[t] = kappa[t - 1] + mu + e[t], with normal innovations whose covariance matrix is estimated from the year-to-year changes (divided by the number of changes minus one), so the innovations are correlated between populations and between orders. This is the random walk with drift of Lee and Carter (1992) for every index, and the multivariate random walk with drift that StMoMo uses for several period indexes (Villegas, Kaishev and Millossovich 2018), here over all populations together. Draws include the innovations and, as in lee_carter(), the uncertainty of the drift (normal, with the innovation covariance divided by the number of changes; StMoMo keeps the drift fixed). Each population has its own drift, so the forecasts of different populations can diverge. Enchev, Kleinow and Cairns (2017, Section 6.2, Table 10) use this process for the population-specific period effects of two variants of the Li-Lee model and note that it lets the populations diverge.

  • index = "coherent": the forecasting model for the CAE model of Enchev, Kleinow and Cairns (2017, Section 6.2, Table 10, Model 3). The period effects of order 1 follow a multivariate random walk with one drift d common to all populations, kappa1[t] = kappa1[t - 1] + d + e1[t], so that the populations do not diverge quickly. The period effects of order 2 follow a vector autoregression of order 1 with a diagonal matrix Phi, which reverts to 0, kappa2[t] = Phi kappa2[t - 1] + e2[t]. The expected log rates of two populations then keep the difference of their first period effects in the last year, and the difference of their second period effects decays to 0, the mean over the fitting years. The variance of the difference of the first period effects still grows with the horizon unless their innovations are perfectly correlated. With one population and order = 1, the draws equal those of index = "rwd".

Choices for index = "coherent" (package-specific; the paper is silent on them).

  • d is the mean year-to-year change of the first period effects over the years and the populations, each population with the same weight (as in the estimation of beta). With common_by, each group has its own drift, from the strata of the group (the bottom strata of a hierarchy); the aggregates of a hierarchy take the drift of their group.

  • Each diagonal element of Phi is the least-squares estimate through the origin for its population, bounded to |phi| <= 0.99 as in li_lee(), because the paper's process is stationary; a warning of class mt_warning_cae names the strata where the bound binds. Orders 3 and higher follow the same process as order 2 (the paper has order = 2).

  • One covariance matrix of the innovations of all populations and orders is estimated from the residuals (divided by the number of changes minus one), as for "rwd". The paper gives each process a volatility matrix, does not say whether the innovations of the two processes are correlated, and reports correlations below 0.3 between them for its data (Section 6.1).

  • Draws include the innovations and the uncertainty of d (normal, with the variance of the mean change), and keep Phi fixed.

Estimation in Enchev, Kleinow and Cairns (2017). The paper fits the CAE model with order = 2 by Poisson maximum likelihood (Section 4.3), with age effects that sum to 1, period effects that sum to 0 over the years for each population, and second period effects that sum to 0 over the populations in each year (Table 4), a constraint that lowers the likelihood (Section 4.2). cae() keeps the least-squares estimates of Kleinow (2015) for both values of index: the period effects are identified by the common principal components, and index = "coherent" applies the paper's forecasting model to them. Rescaling a column of beta leaves the forecasts unchanged. Rotating the age effects changes them, so forecasts from the paper's estimates can differ. The paper's data (men aged 60-89 in six countries, 1961-2010) are not in the Human Mortality Database extracts of demography and StMoMo, and the paper reports its forecasts as figures.

Other package-specific choices.

  • The criterion is minimised by Jacobi rotations (Cardoso and Souloumiac 1996), each of which minimises it in one plane, started from the eigenvectors of the sum of the Q[i], until no rotation of more than 1e-12 radians lowers the criterion by more than 1e-20 times the sum of squares of the matrices (at most 500 sweeps over all pairs of columns; a warning of class mt_warning_cae reports when this limit is reached). The paper uses the F-G algorithm (Flury and Constantine 1985) with the modification of Clarkson (1988). The criterion can have several local minima; the estimate is the one reached from this start.

  • The columns of beta are ordered by the sum over populations of the diagonal elements of t(beta) Q[i] beta. The paper orders them by the diagonal of one population and notes that the order can differ between populations, with no general solution (Section 3.2).

  • Zero deaths are replaced by 0.5 before taking logarithms.

  • common_by (for example "sex") gives each group of strata its own common age effects, estimated from the strata of the group. The paper names this extension and leaves it for further research (Section 3.1). The innovations of the period effects of all strata have one covariance matrix, with correlations across groups.

  • If the data carry a hierarchy (see mt_aggregate_strata()), beta is estimated from the bottom strata only, and the aggregates get their period effects by projection on it, as the other strata (as in li_lee()).

Choice of order. The fit holds the mean squared error of the centred log rates (eq. 4) and the approximate BIC of eq. (5), N log(MSE) + k log(N) with N the number of rates and k = order (K T + n) parameters for K populations, T years and n ages (one beta per group of common_by); mt_parameters() reports them (rows mse and bic). In the paper's application (men in ten countries), order = 2 had the lowest BIC in both age ranges (Table 2). Compare orders also in a backtest.

References

Kleinow T (2015). A common age effect model for the mortality of multiple populations. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 63: 147-152. doi:10.1016/j.insmatheco.2015.03.023

Flury BN (1984). Common principal components in k groups. Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(388): 892-898. doi:10.1080/01621459.1984.10477108

Flury BN, Constantine G (1985). Algorithm AS 211: the F-G diagonalization algorithm. Applied Statistics 34(2): 177-183. doi:10.2307/2347375

Clarkson DB (1988). Remark AS R71: a remark on algorithm AS 211. The F-G diagonalization algorithm. Applied Statistics 37(1): 147-151. doi:10.2307/2347513

Cardoso J-F, Souloumiac A (1996). Jacobi angles for simultaneous diagonalization. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications 17(1): 161-164. doi:10.1137/S0895479893259546

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87(419): 659-671.

Enchev V, Kleinow T, Cairns AJG (2017). Multi-population mortality models: fitting, forecasting and comparisons. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal 2017(4): 319-342. doi:10.1080/03461238.2015.1133450

Villegas AM, Kaishev VK, Millossovich P (2018). StMoMo: an R package for stochastic mortality modeling. Journal of Statistical Software 84(3): 1-38. doi:10.18637/jss.v084.i03

See also

li_lee() and coherent_fdm() for coherent joint models; coupled() to give separate forecasts the dependence of a joint model.

Examples

# more years (30) than age groups (9): ages 50 and over in 5-year groups
x <- mt_subset(mt_regroup(mt_example(), age = "deaths"), ages = c(50, Inf))
fit <- mt_fit(cae(order = 2), x)
p <- mt_parameters(fit)
p[parameter %in% c("mse", "bic")]
#>    stratum parameter  index         value
#>     <char>    <char> <char>         <num>
#> 1:   model       mse         3.047876e-04
#> 2:   model       bic        -3.503547e+03
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
# common drift and mean-reverting second period effects
x2 <- mt_subset(mt_example_regions(years = 1990:2019, regions = 2), ages = c(60, Inf))
fit2 <- mt_fit(cae(order = 2, index = "coherent"), x2)
fit2$fits$common_drift
#> [1] -0.03004355
fc2 <- mt_forecast(fit2, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
